summary: High-stayed videos (47–52% stayed_pct) focus on immediate human body/everyday experiences rather than distant science or engineering topics. Winning hooks use immediate second-person statements ('Your eyes', 'Your leg') that instantly correct a common misconception or state a strange fact happening *right now*. Low-stayed videos (<31% stayed_pct) use slow narrative setups ('Your car swerves...'), vague generalizations ('Most James Webb images hold secrets'), or multi-clause passive introductory sentences. Titles for top performers are concise, direct 5-8 word question/fact statements without unnecessary emoji padding. Keep topic focus strictly anchored to personal, relatable body curiosity to consistently break the 1,200 view threshold.
winning_hooks: Your eyes are leaking right now, and your brain is hiding it.
Your leg doesn't actually fall asleep because of blood loss. It's not blood.
You are not sad when you chop an onion.
avoid: Vague third-person generalizations about distant science (e.g., 'Most James Webb images hold secrets.')
Hypothetical story setups in place of direct facts (e.g., 'Your car swerves off the highway...')
Slow introductory exposition with multi-clause sentences (e.g., 'Fossilized bones can last millions of years, but sometimes...')
next_experiment: A/B test a body-phenomenon topic using a direct misconception hook ('Your stomach isn't actually growling because it's empty') versus an abstract science topic ('Why your stomach acid is strong enough to melt metal') using identical 30-35s lengths and minimal titles.
